summary: Cape Negro Island light at Negro Harbour, Shelburne County, Nova Scotia: lit in 1872, a concrete tower since 1915, owned by the Coast Guard, seen best by boat.

light.fog_signal: horn: blast 6 s, silence 54 s (Coast Guard list)

structures.note: Square wooden lighthouse, 29 ft (Department of Marine 1872 report, quoted by Lighthouse Friends). Standing until replaced.
Wooden octagonal tower, 44 ft. Lighthouse Friends: work began 1886 after a $975 tender from a Mr. DeChamp; heritage statement: built 1887. Both earlier lights stood 1.3 km north of the present one.

Reinforced concrete, tapered octagonal, red and white; 42 ft (12.8 m) base to vane. Contract to D. C. Mulhall, $11,200 (Lighthouse Friends). Built at the southeast end of South Island. Coast Guard list gives the height of the structure above ground as 12.0 m; the heritage statement's 12.8 m is measured base to vane.

staffing.note: Keepers listed to 1965 by Lighthouse Friends. The end of resident keeping is not dated in the sources read.

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds open, tower closed. Best seen by boat (Lighthouse Friends).

events.note: First exhibited 6 September 1872, red and white revolving light (Department of Marine 1872 report, quoted by Lighthouse Friends).
Square wooden lighthouse, 29 ft; contract to James D. Coffin, $970; about $429 for lamps and revolving apparatus.
About two years after the tower went up, $600 provided for a separate keeper's dwelling (Lighthouse Friends).
Old light found too decayed to repair in 1886; work began on a 44 ft wooden octagonal tower (Lighthouse Friends). Heritage statement dates that tower to 1887.
Reinforced concrete octagonal tower at the southeast end of South Island, replacing the wooden tower.
Listed on the Canadian Register of Historic Places (Lighthouse Friends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends says work on the 44 ft wooden octagonal tower began in 1886, after the old light was judged beyond repair. The heritage statement says it was built in 1887. The story gives both.
Lighthouse Friends gives a focal plane of 91 ft above the water (about 27.7 m). The Coast Guard list gives 28.3 m. The story gives the Coast Guard figure as the current one and notes the difference.
The Coast Guard list gives LFl W 6s, which the record also uses. The record's OpenStreetMap and Wikidata characteristics (Fl(2) W 15s; F W) are not supported by the sources read and are not used.
The first light was first exhibited 6 September 1872 (Department report as quoted by Lighthouse Friends). The 1915 date in the record refers to the present concrete tower.

Lighthouse Friends and the heritage statement give 12.8 m (42 ft), the heritage figure measured base to vane. The Coast Guard list gives the structure height above ground as 12.0 m. The story gives both.

The Coast Guard list (entry 349) calls the light Long Rock Light and Fog Signal. It places it on the southeast end of the island at 43 30 26.2 N, 065 20 44.2 W, which is the position Lighthouse Friends gives (43.507278, -65.345611). The story says so.

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence: two heritage and Lighthouse Friends accounts plus Coast Guard list and three Department of Marine keeper tables. Department of Marine 1872 report is not in the corpus; its text is only as Lighthouse Friends quotes it (cited as quoted). Keeper dates for McKinnon and Nickerson come from Lighthouse Friends; the 1906 table's 'Negro Island iJuly 26, 1897' is matched by position in OCR and is the only date from a Department table. Contractor D. C. Mulhall of Liverpool appears in the 1915 Department report's contractor table, but the printed row does not name Negro Island beside him, so the $11,200 contract is attributed to Lighthouse Friends only. Wreck and storm records: none found in the sources read; the Chronicling America search for Negro Island and Nickerson returned nothing relevant. Lighthouse Friends gives 1886 as the start of the wooden tower; the heritage statement gives 1887. Keepers after 1943 are from the heritage statement (to 1963) and Lighthouse Friends (1964 and 1965 only); the record's staffing is unknown. Post-1960 names (Radford Malone, Carmen Cook) are listed in public-role form only. Web searches: 1. Page reads: about 6. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1903, 1906 and 1907 keeper tables were read on the page images, not only the OCR. The 1906 row reads Nickerson, Byron / Negro Island / July 26, 1897 (salary 300.00).
